I agree this is a real need, and painful to do today. I also want to compliment you on a very good proposal that follows all aspects of [the process for proposing new features](https://wiki.whatwg.org/wiki/FAQ#Is_there_a_process_for_adding_new_features_to_a_specification.3F), e.g. listing requirements, illustrating current workarounds, and staying away from particular API suggestions.

Now we just need to get implementer interest in solving this problem... I'll try reaching out. We might along the way find out that there's a better solution using existing technology, of course. From the Chromium side, maybe @garykac to start? (Actually, now that I think about it, this might make more sense as a proposal for https://w3c.github.io/uievents/ , which Gary edits --- but we can certainly start the discussion here.)

Would you consider browser shortcuts in scope here? For example, in Firefox, "/" starts an in-page search (in addition to triggering a keypress event for "/"). So, would such an API always return true in Firefox? Or do you think we should solve this problem for "element-specific" behavior separately?

> I also want to compliment you on a very good proposal that follows all aspects of the process for proposing new features ... staying away from particular API suggestions

Thanks! I tried hard to do this, specifically avoiding the words which would allude to my own perceived solution - which I'll try to continue to do 😛

> Would you consider browser shortcuts in scope here?

Yes - absolutely. The priority here is to _not conflict_ with users expectations of what their software already does.

> So, would such an API always return true in Firefox?

`true` perhaps, or perhaps another positive signal. Perhaps an enum to determine how... visible/high priority(?) the native action is? Perhaps an enum of behaviour categories? I'm thinking it could be useful to determine what _kind_ of behaviour the browser would natively do; for example we _definitely_ don't want to override users inputting text into a textarea, but might want to override search functionality (i.e. ctrl/cmd+f) in, for example a text editor webapp.

> Or do you think we should solve this problem for "element-specific" behavior separately

Why not both? The _intent_ is to not conflict with browsers native behaviour - which includes both global shortcuts and element based ones. Perhaps, again, some mechanism to determine which type the native behaviour would be could be useful.

Hi Keith, we've been thinking about reserved keys a lot recently - primarily to make these keys available for webapps like remote access/remote shell. Basically, we wanted to add a mechanism to make these special keys available to webapps that need them.

tl;dr: We have a proposal (see link at bottom) that seems like it addresses some of your concerns. Chrome is currently working on an implementation of the proposal.

But before getting to that, I wanted to provide some background info about our thinking process while working on the proposal.

We divided the reserved keys into 2 groups: **browser keys** (reserved by the UA, like Esc or Ctrl-w), and **system keys** (reserved by the OS, like Alt-Tab).

- Browser keys are "easy" in that the UA just needs to send them along and bypass special handling.
- System keys are more difficult since they may require that the UA add special handlers to grab these keys from the OS (since they aren't normally passed along to the UA).

Problems we considered/encountered:

- We didn't feel that knowing the reserved keys for the current OS/UA was sufficient. For many use cases, you need to know the union of all reserved keys for all OSs and UAs.
   - For example, if a webapp allows a user to use/override ctrl-w because they're connecting from a Mac, if they next connect from a Windows machine, what is the expected behavior?
   - But it's not reasonable for UAs to maintain a list of keys reserved by all other UAs. A list like that feels more appropriate for an external JS library.
- Security: Being able to override some browser keys has security concerns because (for example) a malicious app that enters fullscreen and overrides Esc would be a very poor user experience. One of the biggest challenges we encountered while working on the proposal was address concerns around API abuse.
   - Summary of comments at TPAC when discussing this proposal: "Sounds useful. Sounds scary."

Here is the proposal that I believe partially addresses your concerns:
- https://w3c.github.io/keyboard-lock/
- [Original explainer](https://github.com/jondahlke/system-keyboard-lock/blob/master/EXPLAINER.md)

Basically, it's an API that allows you to request certain key combinations (or all key combos) to be sent to the app. Because of security concerns, it is restricted to Fullscreen only. We hope to be able to remove that restriction at some point in the future (as was done for [mouse lock](https://www.chromium.org/developers/design-documents/mouse-lock)), but the API needs to prove itself first.

Note that the proposal doesn't address your concern about being able to detect when an override would be shadowing existing UA behavior.

Please let us know what you think. And file bugs/comments at: https://github.com/w3c/keyboard-lock

OHAI @keithamus funny seeing you here :-). Also ran into this last year but chalked it up to my lack of understanding. Great example on submitting a proposal. Now i know how NOT to push your own agenda while pushing an agenda. #salute. /cc @brandondees
